body: Welcome. Over about ninety days you will get one short note a day to help you step away from constant switching and grow into calm, unhurried focus.
Before changing anything, simply notice how often you switch tasks today. Counting the hops is the first step towards fewer of them.
Distraction is not a character flaw. Most of our tools are designed to pull at attention, so struggling with focus is a normal response.
Watch what you reach for in the first minute of boredom. That reflex shows you where your attention habitually escapes.
Notice the small itch to check something just as a task gets difficult. Switching often begins exactly where effort starts.
Deep focus is less about willpower and more about conditions. Over these weeks you will build those conditions, piece by piece.
Pay attention to when your mind feels clearest. Morning, afternoon or late evening, your best hour is worth protecting.
Count how many tabs and windows are open on your screen right now. Each one is a small, quiet request for your attention.
Notice how a single interruption can cost far more than the moment itself. Getting back into the work often takes a while.
Being busy and being focused feel similar but are quite different. One scatters your energy; the other gathers it.
Spot one notification that interrupted you this morning. Ask yourself whether it truly needed to reach you at that moment.
Remember a time you lost track of the clock because you were absorbed. That capacity is still in you, waiting for room.
Write down the one task that would make tomorrow feel worthwhile. Knowing it in advance makes starting much easier.
Set a timer for fifteen minutes and work on a single thing until it rings. Nothing else is allowed in during that time.
Put your phone in another room for one work session. Notice how often your hand reaches for it anyway.
Close every tab you do not need for the task at hand. A tidy screen makes a quieter mind.
Turn off one notification you have never really needed. One fewer ping is one less thread pulling at you.
Keep a scrap of paper beside you as you work. When a stray thought arrives, write it down and return to the task.
Try starting your day with the important task before opening email or messages. Let the first hour belong to you.
Restlessness is normal when you first sit with one thing. Let it rise and fall, like a wave, without obeying it.
Stretch your timer to twenty minutes of single-task work. Small increases build stamina without making focus feel like a punishment.
Tell a colleague or housemate that you will be unavailable for half an hour. Protected time is easier to keep when others know.
Clear your desk of everything except what this task needs. Physical clutter tends to tug at attention more than we realise.
Before you begin, write one sentence describing what done looks like for this session. A clear finish line helps you stay on track.
Batch your messages: reply to them all at two set times rather than as they arrive.
Sit quietly for two minutes before you start work, just following your breath. A settled mind slips into focus more easily.
Use a single window in full screen for your next session. Hiding everything else removes a dozen tiny temptations.
Notice the moment you want to switch, then wait ten breaths before deciding. Often the urge simply fades.
When focus slips, there is no need to scold yourself. Gently bring your attention back, as many times as it takes.
Try working with background noise that has no words, such as rain sounds or quiet instrumental music. See how it affects your concentration.
Take a proper break after a focused block: stand, stretch and look out of a window. Rest is part of deep work, not a reward for it.
Plan tomorrow's focus block tonight and put it in your calendar. A scheduled appointment with yourself is harder to give away.
Choose one app to remove from your phone's home screen. A little friction can stop a lot of absent-minded checking.
Read something long and demanding for twenty minutes without skimming. Slow reading strengthens the same muscle as deep work.
Begin your focus session with a tiny ritual, like making tea or clearing your desk. Rituals signal to your mind that it is time to settle.
Try thirty minutes of single-task work. If you drift, simply note it on paper and carry on.
Switch off email entirely for one hour this morning. The messages will wait, and so will the world.
Notice which tasks make you most eager to escape. Often they are the ones that matter most.
Break a large task into the very next physical action. It is much easier to focus on writing one paragraph than on finishing a report.
Keep a simple tally of how many focused blocks you complete this week. Seeing progress builds quiet confidence.
For one meal, eat without a screen. Paying attention to a simple thing is practice for paying attention to harder ones.
Try a forty-minute session with your phone switched off, not just silenced. Notice how the room feels different.
Write by hand for ten minutes about what you are working on. Pen and paper can slow your thinking to a useful pace.
Ask yourself before opening any app what you came for. If you cannot answer, close it again.
Set up your workspace the night before, so the morning starts with the work rather than preparation.
Try a walk without headphones or podcasts. Letting your mind wander freely is good rest for focused attention.
Notice the difference between how you feel after scrolling and after focused work. Your mood can be a useful guide.
When an urgent thought pulls at you mid-session, ask whether it will still matter in an hour. Most things can wait.
Choose one meeting or call this week to attend with your full attention, with no other windows open.
Aim for a forty-five minute block of focus on your most important task. Protect it as you would an important appointment.
Deep work feels slower at first, yet it often produces more. Trust the unhurried pace while it builds.
Let a difficult problem stay difficult for a few minutes longer than feels comfortable. Breakthroughs tend to hide just past the urge to quit.
Spend the first five minutes of a session simply reviewing where you left off. Re-entry is easier with a gentle warm-up.
Try leaving a task mid-sentence when you stop for the day. Tomorrow you will know exactly where to pick up.
Put away the second screen or device for a whole morning. One surface, one task, one stream of thought.
Notice what tires your attention: poor sleep, hunger, too much caffeine. Look after the body that does the focusing.
Silence group chats for the working day and check them once at lunch. Nothing important will be lost.
Go for a full hour on one task, with a short stretch break halfway if you need it. You are closer than you think.
Reflect on your best focus session so far. What conditions made it possible, and how can you recreate them?
Try a session at a library or quiet café where you have nothing else to do but the work.
When you feel stuck, stay with the problem by sketching it on paper rather than searching online. Thinking slowly often beats looking things up.
Turn your phone face down and out of reach during conversations. Focused attention on people is part of the same practice.
Keep a short log after each focus block: what you did and how deep it felt. Patterns will start to emerge.
Notice that focus gets easier once you are ten minutes in. Starting is the hardest part, so make starting simple.
Choose a single project for your mornings this week and give it your full attention. Depth comes from returning again and again.
When you finish a block, write down the very next step before standing up. You are leaving a gift for your future self.
Protect two focused hours in your diary this week, and decline anything that tries to land on top of them.
Practise being bored for five minutes while waiting, without picking up your phone. Boredom is where patience grows.
You no longer need perfect conditions to concentrate. Each session you have done has made focusing a little more natural.
Look back at your first notes about switching. Compare that scattered week with how your attention feels now.
Work for an hour on something that really matters to you. Notice the calm that settles once you are fully inside it.
Being someone who focuses is less about strict rules and more about what you return to. Keep returning.
Review which habits have helped most, such as the phone in another room or the morning block. Keep those as your defaults.
Explain to a friend how you protect your attention. Saying it aloud helps it become part of who you are.
Notice how your work feels when you give it undivided time. There is often more care in it, and more satisfaction too.
Allow yourself an unhurried session where you aim for quality rather than speed. Let the work take the time it needs.
Distractions will always exist. What has changed is that you now notice them and choose, rather than simply follow.
Plan next week's focused blocks before this one ends. A rhythm you plan ahead is far easier to keep.
Spend an evening on a hobby with your full attention, with no screens nearby. Focus is a gift for leisure as well as work.
Think about what an hour of deep focus has made possible for you lately. Those hours add up to real achievement.
If a busy week scatters your attention, begin again with one short session. The skill does not vanish; it just needs a nudge.
Choose the default settings you want to keep for good: notifications off, one tab, one task. Make them part of your normal day.
You can now sit with one task for an hour. That once felt out of reach, and today it is simply part of who you are.
Share one focus habit with someone who seems overwhelmed. Teaching it quietly reinforces it in you.
Notice the steadiness that deep work brings to the rest of your day. Calm attention spills over into conversations, meals and rest.
Give your next focused hour to something that will still matter in a year. Depth is best spent on what endures.
Your attention is one of the most valuable things you own. You have learnt to spend it on purpose.
When the pull to switch appears, you now know it is only a feeling. You can let it pass and stay with what matters.
Take one more full hour of focus this week and savour it. Think of it as a celebration of how far you have come.
Look back over these ninety days. What have you discovered about your attention that you want to remember?
You began by counting distractions and now you protect whole hours. Be proud of the patient work that took.
This is the last note. You have become someone who can focus deeply and calmly, and that steady attention is yours to keep.
